About this tracker

This tool keeps an eye on Microsoft's Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), AKS Application Network, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes, AKS Arc, Kubernetes Fleet Manager, Azure Linux, Azure Container Registry (ACR), and Azure Application Gateway for Containers (AGC) documentation. AKS everywhere! It also shows the last 5 AKS and App Net release notes.

It automatically scans for changes, then uses AI to summarize and highlight updates that are most likely to matter — such as new features, deprecations, and significant content revisions.

Minor edits (like typos, formatting tweaks, and other low-impact changes) are usually filtered out. Because the process is automated, some updates may be missed or summaries may not capture every nuance.

For complete accuracy, you can always follow the provided links to the original Microsoft documentation.

With this tracker, you can:

  • Quickly scan meaningful AKS, AKS Automatic, AKS Support, App Net, Arc K8s, AKS Arc, Azure Linux, ACR, AGC, and Fleet documentation changes from the past 7 days
  • Stay up to date with the latest AKS and App Net release notes without digging through every doc page
  • Search and browse CVE security data across AKS releases and VHD node images, powered by the AKS Vulnerability Data API (Public Preview)

Get the Latest AKS Docs - Every Week, in Your Inbox

updated: 04/11/2026, 18:58:56

Release 2026-10-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-27

The release on 2026-10-25 introduces automatic upgrades for unsupported Kubernetes versions and updates to node pools.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will automatically upgrade unsupported clusters after a grace period.
  • Default OS SKU for node pools changes to Ubuntu 26.04 with Kubernetes 1.38.
🔑

Key Features

  • Kubernetes 1.37 is now generally available as Long-Term Support.
  • Node Auto Provisioning (NAP) enhancements include new CRDs and features.
💡

Good to Know

  • Review upgrade channels to prepare for automated upgrades.
  • Community support for Kubernetes 1.34 ends by November 2026.

Release Notes 2026-09-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-01

The 2026-09-25 release introduces significant updates and deprecations. Key features include the general availability of identity bindings and preview support for Ubuntu 26.04.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • Windows Server 2022 is not supported in Kubernetes version 1.37 and above.
  • Flatcar Container Linux node images are removed, affecting scaling operations.
  • The annotation service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-pip-tags no longer overrides public IP tags.
🔑

Key Features

  • Identity bindings are now generally available.
  • Ubuntu 26.04 is available in preview.
  • Windows Server OS SKU migration to 2025 is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • AKS will auto-migrate deprecated Availability Sets clusters after September 30, 2026.
  • AKS release order has been updated for Central US and East US.
  • Check AKS Release Tracker for detailed release timing.

Release 2026-09-04

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-09-09

This release introduces Kubernetes 1.37 and autoscaling for VM node pools. It also announces the retirement of Azure Linux with OS Guard.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will remove Azure Linux with OS Guard node images on March 10, 2027.
  • AKS no longer produces VHDs for Windows Server 2019 and version 23H2.
🔑

Key Features

  • Autoscaling for Virtual Machines node pools is now generally available.
  • Kubernetes patch versions 1.36.3, 1.35.7, and 1.34.10 are available.
  • On-Demand Monitor for node health checks is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • LocalDNS is enabled automatically for compatible cluster networking.
  • AKS rejects updates that remove IPv6 from dual-stack clusters.
  • Managed namespace creation rejects names starting with reserved prefixes.

AppNet 2026-08-19

App Net
View Release
📅 2026-08-31

AppNet is now in public preview with several updates and bug fixes.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AppNet 1.0, 1.1, and 1.2 versions retired.
  • Moving AppNet resources across resource groups is now blocked.
🔑

Key Features

  • AppNet available in more Azure regions.
  • AppNet 1.5 updated to Istio 1.30.3.
💡

Good to Know

  • Cluster prerequisites validated at member-join time.
  • Fixed issues with member updates and version upgrades.

Release 2026-08-07

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-08-11

This release introduces several enhancements including Node Auto Provisioning and automatic availability zone placement.

🔑

Key Features

  • Node Auto Provisioning now supports restricted public network access
  • Automatic availability zone placement is enabled globally
  • Control-plane only upgrades to AKS Long Term Support are allowed
  • Node pool rollback feature is now generally available
  • Encryption in Transit for Azure File CSI driver is now available

Documentation Updates

Meaningful updates to AKS, AKS Automatic, AKS Support, App Net, Arc K8s, AKS Arc, Azure Linux, ACR, AGC, and Fleet docs from the last 7 days.

Register the resource provider.++    ```azurecli+    az provider register --namespace Microsoft.HybridConnectivity --subscription <subscription-id>+    ```+4. Retry the cluster creation.+ ## Upgrade remains in progress  Wait up to 30 minutes, then confirm that the host remains connected to Azure Arc.                                                                                                                                                                                         @@ -2,45 +2,323 @@  ## Summary -This article discusses how to identify and resolve the `K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError` error (also known as error code ERR\_K8S\_API\_SERVER\_CONN\_FAIL, error number 51) that occurs when you try to start or create and deploy a Microsoft Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster.+This article describes how to identify and resolve the `K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError` error (also known as error code `ERR_K8S_API_SERVER_CONN_FAIL`, error number 51). This error might occur when you create, start, scale, or upgrade a Microsoft Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster or node pool.++When AKS provisions a Linux node, the node bootstrap script (delivered through the `vmssCSE` Custom Script Extension) checks whether the node can reach the cluster's Kubernetes API server on TCP port 443 before it starts the kubelet. If the node can resolve the API server address but can't establish a connection to it, the script exits with code 51, the node isn't registered in the cluster, and the operation fails.++In most cases, this error is caused by a network configuration in the customer's environment (such as a firewall, network security group, route table, proxy, or authorized IP range) that blocks or drops traffic from the node subnet to the API server.++Note++- This article applies to Linux nodes. If the node can't *resolve* the API server name, you receive a different error. For more information, see [Troubleshoot the K8SAPIServerDNSLookupFailVMExtensionError error code (52)](error-code-k8sapiserverdnslookupfailvmextensionerror). If the node can't reach required outbound endpoints such as `mcr.microsoft.com`, see [Troubleshoot the OutboundConnFailVMExtensionError error code (50)](error-code-outboundconnfailvmextensionerror).+- If your cluster uses [API Server VNet Integration](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-vnet-integration), a blocked connection to the API server usually causes a different error. See Clusters that use API Server VNet Integration.  ## Prerequisites -- The [Netcat](https://linuxcommandlibrary.com/man/netcat) (nc) command-line tool+- [Azure CLI](/en-us/cli/azure/install-azure-cli), signed in to the subscription that contains the AKS cluster.+- Permissions to read the AKS cluster and to run commands on the virtual machine scale sets (VMSS) or virtual machines (VMs) in the cluster's node resource group (for example, the [Virtual Machine Contributor](/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles/compute#virtual-machine-contributor) role).++The connectivity tests in this article run on the AKS nodes by using [Azure Run Command](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/linux/run-command). They use the [curl](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html) command-line tool (or [Netcat](https://linuxcommandlibrary.com/man/netcat) (`nc`) for clusters that use API Server VNet Integration). These tools are already included in AKS Linux node images, so you don't have to install them on your local computer or on the nodes.  ## Symptoms -When you try to start or create an AKS cluster, you receive the following error message:-->-> Unable to establish connection from agents to Kubernetes API server, please see https://aka.ms/aks-required-ports-and-addresses for more information.->-> Details: Code="VMExtensionProvisioningError"->-> Message="VM has reported a failure when processing extension 'vmssCSE'.->-> Error message: "**Enable failed: failed to execute command: command terminated with exit status=51**\n[stdout]\n{->-> "ExitCode": "51",->-> "Output": "Thu Oct 14 18:07:37 UTC 2021,aks-nodepool1-18315663-vmss000000\nConnection to+When you try to create, start, scale, or upgrade an AKS cluster or node pool, the operation fails and you receive an error message that resembles the following example (identifiers are replaced with placeholders, and repeated progress output is removed):++```output+Code: K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError+Message: Create or update VMSS <vmss-resource-id> failed. Multiple VM extensions failed to be provisioned on the VM. The Extensions failed due to the errors:++[Extension Name: '<vmss-name>-AKSLinuxBilling'+Error Message: The handler for VM extension type 'Microsoft.AKS.Compute.AKS.Linux.Billing' has reported terminal failure for VM extension '<vmss-name>-AKSLinuxBilling' with error message: 'Dependent Extension Microsoft.Azure.Extensions.CustomScript did not succeed. Status was error'.]++[Extension Name: 'vmssCSE'+Error Message: VM has reported a user failure when processing extension 'vmssCSE'. Please correct the error and try again. (publisher 'Microsoft.Azure.Extensions' and type 'CustomScript'). Error code: '2'. This error is a side effect of the `vmssCSE` failure, not a separate problem.++In some API versions or tools, the message might begin with `Unable to establish connection from agents to Kubernetes API server, please see https://aka.ms/aks-required-ports-and-addresses for more information.` followed by `Code="VMExtensionProvisioningError"`.  ## Cause -Your cluster nodes can't connect to your cluster API server pod.+During node provisioning, the bootstrap script validates connectivity from the node to the API server before it starts the kubelet:++| Cluster configuration | Address that the node uses | Check performed by the bootstrap script |+| --- | --- | --- |+| Public cluster | Public API server FQDN (`<dns-prefix>-<hash>.hcp.<region>.azmk8s.io`) | DNS lookup, then `curl https://<api-server-fqdn>:443` (with retries) |+| Private cluster | Private API server FQDN (for example, `<dns-prefix>-<hash>.<guid>.privatelink.<region>.azmk8s.io`) that resolves to the private endpoint IP | DNS lookup, then `curl https://<api-server-fqdn>:443` (with retries) |++If the DNS lookup fails, the script exits with code 52 or 53. If the DNS lookup succeeds but the TCP/TLS connection to port 443 can't be established within the retry period, the script exits with code 51.++The node must be able to reach the API server for AKS to work. This requirement is documented in [Outbound network and FQDN rules for AKS clusters](/en-us/azure/aks/outbound-rules-control-egress#azure-global-required-fqdn--application-rules): `*.hcp.<location>.azmk8s.io` on HTTPS port 443 is required for node-to-API server communication.++Common reasons why the connection fails include:++- **Egress filtering blocks the API server.** A firewall, network virtual appliance (NVA), or proxy on the egress path doesn't allow TCP 443 to the API server FQDN (`*.hcp.<region>.azmk8s.io`) or to the API server public IP address.+- **TLS inspection or a proxy interferes with the connection.** A device that intercepts, decrypts, or rewrites TLS traffic (including the Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) extension) to the API server breaks the connection.+- **Network security group (NSG) rules deny the traffic.** An outbound rule on the node subnet or NIC blocks TCP 443 from the nodes to the API server.+- **User-defined routes (UDRs) send traffic to the wrong next hop.** A route table on the node subnet sends API server traffic to an NVA that drops it, routes it asymmetrically, or has no path to the destination.+- **API server authorized IP ranges don't include the cluster's egress IP.** If [authorized IP ranges](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-authorized-ip-ranges) are enabled and the nodes egress through an IP address that isn't in the list (for example, the public IP of an Azure Firewall, NAT gateway, or other NVA), the API server rejects the connection.+- **(Private clusters) The private FQDN resolves to the wrong IP address.** Custom DNS servers or a manually managed private DNS zone return an outdated or incorrect IP address, so the node connects to an address where the API server isn't listening.+- **(Private clusters) The node can't reach the private endpoint.** For example, NSG rules or UDRs block traffic to the private endpoint IP, or the private endpoint is in a peered VNet that isn't reachable from the node subnet.  ## Solution -Run a Netcat command to verify that your nodes can resolve the cluster's fully qualified domain name (FQDN):+### Step 1: Gather cluster information++1. Get the API server endpoints and the network configuration of the cluster by running the [az aks show](/en-us/cli/azure/aks#az-aks-show) command:++    ```azurecli+    az aks show \+        --resource-group <resource-group> \+        --name <cluster-name> \+        --query "{fqdn:fqdn, privateFqdn:privateFqdn, nodeResourceGroup:nodeResourceGroup, outboundType:networkProfile.outboundType, privateCluster:apiServerAccessProfile.enablePrivateCluster, vnetIntegration:apiServerAccessProfile.enableVnetIntegration, authorizedIpRanges:apiServerAccessProfile.authorizedIpRanges}" \+        --output json+    ```++    Use the output to determine the API server FQDN that the nodes use:++    - **Public cluster**: Use the `fqdn` value.+    - **Private cluster**: Use the `privateFqdn` value. If `privateFqdn` is empty (for example, when the private DNS zone is set to `none`), use the `fqdn` value.++    If `vnetIntegration` is `true`, see Clusters that use API Server VNet Integration instead.++    The error message usually contains the API server FQDN that the node tried to reach (for example, `Failed to connect to <api-server-fqdn> port 443`).+2. Identify the node pool instances that failed provisioning.++    - For node pools that use **Virtual Machine Scale Sets** (default):++        ```azurecli+        az vmss list \+            --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+            --query "[].{name:name, nodePool:tags.\"aks-managed-poolName\", provisioningState:provisioningState}" \+            --output table++        az vmss list-instances \+            --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+            --name <vmss-name> \+            --query "[].{instanceId:instanceId, name:name, provisioningState:provisioningState}" \+            --output table+        ```+    - For [Virtual Machines node pools](/en-us/azure/aks/virtual-machines-node-pools):++        ```azurecli+        az vm list \+            --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+            --query "[?tags.\"aks-managed-poolName\"=='<node-pool-name>'].{name:name, provisioningState:provisioningState}" \+            --output table+        ```++### Step 2: Test connectivity from the node to the API server++Because the node didn't register in the cluster, you can't use `kubectl debug` to access it. Instead, use [Azure Run Command](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/linux/run-command) to run the same check that the bootstrap script runs.++Note++- The VM or VMSS instance must still exist and be running. If AKS already removed the failed instance, run the tests from a test VM that you deploy in the same node subnet (with the same NSG and route table).+- Run Command returns only the last 4,096 bytes of output, and only one Run Command can run on a VM at a time.+- The `--query "value[0].message" --output tsv` parameters in the following commands print the command output as readable text instead of JSON.++The following command is the same check that the bootstrap script runs. It sends an HTTPS request to the API server FQDN by using the cluster certificate authority (`/etc/kubernetes/certs/ca.crt`) that's already on the node. The verbose (`-v`) output shows the IP address that the FQDN resolves to and where the connection fails, so a separate DNS lookup isn't required. The `--max-time 30` parameter stops the test after 30 seconds if the API server doesn't respond.++- For a **Virtual Machine Scale Sets** node pool, run the [az vmss run-command invoke](/en-us/cli/azure/vmss/run-command#az-vmss-run-command-invoke) command:++    ```azurecli+    az vmss run-command invoke \+        --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+        --name <vmss-name> \+        --instance-id <instance-id> \+        --command-id RunShellScript \+        --scripts "curl -v --max-time 30 --cacert /etc/kubernetes/certs/ca.crt https://<api-server-fqdn>:443" \+        --query "value[0].message" \+        --output tsv+    ```+- For a **Virtual Machines** node pool, run the [az vm run-command invoke](/en-us/cli/azure/vm/run-command#az-vm-run-command-invoke) command:++    ```azurecli+    az vm run-command invoke \+        --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+        --name <vm-name> \+        --command-id RunShellScript \+        --scripts "curl -v --max-time 30 --cacert /etc/kubernetes/certs/ca.crt https://<api-server-fqdn>:443" \+        --query "value[0].message" \+        --output tsv+    ```++If the node can reach the API server, the `[stdout]` section contains an `Unauthorized` response from the API server, and the `[stderr]` section shows a successful connection. The `401` response is expected because the request is anonymous. The following example is abbreviated: -```shell-nc -vz <cluster-fqdn> 443+```output+Enable succeeded:+[stdout]+{+  "kind": "Status",+  "apiVersion": "v1",+  "metadata": {},+  "status": "Failure",+  "message": "Unauthorized",+  "reason": "Unauthorized",+  "code": 401+}+[stderr]+* Host <api-server-fqdn>:443 was resolved.+* IPv4: <api-server-ip>+*   Trying <api-server-ip>:443...+* Connected to <api-server-fqdn> (<api-server-ip>) port 443+...+*  SSL certificate verify ok.+...+< HTTP/2 401+... ``` -If you're using egress filtering through a firewall, make sure that traffic is allowed to your cluster FQDN.+If the node can't reach the API server, the `[stdout]` section is empty and curl reports the error at the end of the `[stderr]` section. For example:++```output+Enable succeeded:+[stdout]++[stderr]+* Host <api-server-fqdn>:443 was resolved.+* IPv4: <api-server-ip>+*   Trying <api-server-ip>:443...+* Connection timed out after 30001 milliseconds+* Closing connection+curl: (28) Connection timed out after 30001 milliseconds+```++Note++`Enable succeeded` only means that Run Command ran the script. It doesn't mean that the connectivity test passed.++#### Review the node provisioning log (optional)++To see the exact command and output of the failed check, review the end of the node provisioning log:++```azurecli+az vmss run-command invoke \+    --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+    --name <vmss-name> \+    --instance-id <instance-id> \+    --command-id RunShellScript \+    --scripts "grep -E 'curl -v --cacert|API server connection check code' /var/log/azure/cluster-provision.log | tail -n 20" \+    --query "value[0].message" \+    --output tsv+```++For a Virtual Machines node pool, use `az vm run-command invoke --resource-group <node-resource-group> --name <vm-name>` with the same `--command-id`, `--scripts`, `--query`, and `--output` values.++### Step 3: Interpret the results++| Result | Meaning | Next step |+| --- | --- | --- |+| curl returns an HTTP response (for example, `HTTP/2 401` with an `Unauthorized` status) | The node can now reach the API server. The issue might have been transient or already fixed. | Retry the operation (see Step 5). |+| `curl: (6) Could not resolve host` | The node can't resolve the API server name. | See [Troubleshoot the K8SAPIServerDNSLookupFailVMExtensionError error code (52)](error-code-k8sapiserverdnslookupfailvmextensionerror). |+| The IP address in the `IPv4:` or `Trying` line isn't the expected API server IP address (private clusters) | DNS returns an incorrect or outdated record. | Verify that the private DNS zone record matches the private endpoint IP and that custom DNS servers forward the zone to Azure DNS (`168.63.129.16`). See [Private AKS clusters](/en-us/azure/aks/private-clusters). |+| `curl: (28)` (`Connection timed out` or `Operation timed out`) | Packets are dropped on the path (NSG, firewall, NVA, UDR, or authorized IP ranges). | Go to Step 4. |+| `curl: (7)` (`Connection refused`), `curl: (35)` or `curl: (56)` (`Connection reset by peer`) | A device on the path actively rejects or resets the connection, or the node connects to the wrong IP address. | Check firewalls, proxies, and NVAs on the path, and verify the resolved IP address. |+| A TLS error, such as `curl: (60) SSL certificate problem` or `curl: (35) ... unexpected eof while reading` | A proxy or TLS inspection device intercepts the connection. | Exclude the API server FQDN from TLS inspection, and don't modify the ALPN extension. |++### Step 4: Fix the network configuration++Based on the cluster configuration, verify the following items.++Tip++To check Azure networking resources (NSGs, route tables, Azure Firewall, NAT gateway, load balancer, and VNet peering) along the path from a node pool to a destination, you can also run a connectivity analysis by using [Azure Virtual Network Verifier](/en-us/azure/virtual-network-manager/concept-virtual-network-verifier). This tool doesn't evaluate third-party or on-premises devices.++#### Public clusters++- If you restrict egress traffic through a firewall or NVA, allow TCP 443 to `*.hcp.<region>.azmk8s.io` (application rule) or to the API server public IP address (network rule). For the complete list of requirements, see [Outbound network and FQDN rules for AKS clusters](/en-us/azure/aks/outbound-rules-control-egress) and [Limit network traffic with Azure Firewall in AKS](/en-us/azure/aks/limit-egress-traffic).+- Make sure that NSGs on the node subnet and node NICs don't deny outbound TCP 443 to the API server.+- Make sure that TLS inspection and proxies don't intercept or alter traffic to the API server FQDN.+- If API server authorized IP ranges are enabled, make sure that the public IP address that the nodes use for egress (for example, the Azure Firewall, NAT gateway, or NVA public IP) is included. Then, retry the operation that failed (create, start, scale, or upgrade). If the cluster or node pool remains in a failed state, you can reconcile the cluster by running the [az aks update](/en-us/cli/azure/aks#az-aks-update) command without other parameters:++```azurecli+az aks update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <cluster-name>+```++## Clusters that use API Server VNet Integration++In clusters that use [API Server VNet Integration](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-vnet-integration), the nodes connect directly to the private IP address of the API server internal load balancer in the delegated API server subnet, without a DNS lookup. Get the private IP address of the API server. The IP address also appears in the error message (`nc -vz <api-server-ip> 443`).++    ```azurecli+    az network lb show \+        --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+        --name kube-apiserver \+        --query "frontendIPConfigurations[].privateIPAddress" \+        --output tsv+    ```+2. Test the connection from an affected node by running the same Netcat check that the bootstrap script runs. It doesn't change t  **Symptom:** Installation fails. The error message starts with `managed KubeRay preflight failed: detected existing KubeRay operator`. -**Cause:** Preview doesn't support same-cluster, in-place adoption of a self-hosted KubeRay operator. KubeRay requires a single operator per cluster. The managed extension rejects installation if it detects a self-hosted or otherwise unmanaged operator.+**Cause:** Preview doesn't support the in-place adoption of a self-hosted KubeRay operator on the same cluster. KubeRay requires a single operator per cluster. The managed extension rejects installation if it detects a self-hosted or otherwise unmanaged operator. The failed installation might update or claim the Ray CRDs before the extension detects the existing operator. -**Resolution:**+**Resolution:** Use this procedure only if both of the following conditions are true: -1. Stop retries on the affected cluster. Rejection doesn't prove that the existing CRDs are unchanged.-2. Keep required workload data, manifests, Ray CRDs, and user-created resources.-3. Collect the diagnostics in the following section before making further changes.-4. Request guidance from Azure support before you uninstall an operator, delete a failed extension, or change CRD ownership.-5. For a new managed installation, use a clean target cluster with no KubeRay installation. Alternatively, [uninstall the self-hosted operator first](/en-us/azure/aks/kuberay-overview#uninstall-an-existing-oss-kuberay-operator). Removal of the operator is a prerequisite. It's not a supported in-place adoption procedure.-6. On an affected cluster, resolve the CRD state with Azure support before making another managed installation attempt.+- The failed managed extension resource still exists.+- A Helm release installed the self-hosted operator. -Warning+This procedure keeps the current CRDs and transfers reconciliation to the managed operator. This migration path isn't supported. If you use this procedure, proceed at your own risk. The procedure minimizes workload disruption, but the operator gap still introduces risk.++1. Stop all repeated extension create, update, and delete requests.+2. Stop new Ray control-plane changes.+3. If possible, wait for active `RayJob` resources to finish. -Don't force CRD ownership transfers, rewrite ownership metadata, or delete Ray CRDs or workload namespaces to recover. If you delete a CRD, you also delete its custom resources.+    Existing Ray pods can continue to run during a short operator gap. During the gap, reconciliation, healing, autoscaling, and `RayJob` status transitions stop.+4. Set values for the existing self-hosted operator release: -A known safety issue can change Ray CRD schemas, labels, and field ownership before the conflicting-operator check rejects installation. If your cluster still uses `basic`, update it with `az aks update --load-balancer-sku standard`.+    - **Node resource group restriction level**: For an AKS-managed virtual network, you need to create a subnet in the node resource group. If the restriction level is `ReadOnly`, set it to `Unrestricted` before you continue. You lock it down again in a later step.+3. Review the changes that disrupt running workloads or access, and plan a maintenance window:++    - Changing the outbound type changes your cluster's egress IP addresses. Update any firewall rules that allow traffic from the cluster.+    - Enabling API Server VNet Integration changes the API server IP address and requires a cluster restart. This change is permanent.+    - Changing the network dataplane, OS SKU, and SSH access settings reimages your nodes.+    - Disabling local accounts removes static kubeconfig credentials. Ensure you have access through Microsoft Entra ID and an Azure RBAC role, such as *Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin*, before you disable them.+    - The migration enables Deployment Safeguards in `Enforce` mode with baseline Pod Security Standards. Deployments that don't comply are rejected. You can exclude namespaces, but you can't switch the cluster-wide level to `Warn`. Review your workloads before you migrate. For more information, see [Use Deployment Safeguards](../deployment-safeguards#excluding-namespaces).++### Prepare cluster networking++1. **Outbound type**: For an AKS-managed virtual network, the outbound type must be a managed NAT gateway. The `loadBalancer` outbound type isn't supported. If needed, update the outbound type:++    ```azurecli+    az aks update \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --outbound-type managedNATGateway \+        --outbound-type-sku StandardV2+    ```++    For a custom virtual network, any outbound type is supported and no change is required. For more information, see [Update outboundType after cluster creation](../egress-outboundtype#update-outboundtype-after-cluster-creation).+2. **Cluster identity**: For an AKS-managed virtual network, keep the cluster's system-assigned managed identity. For a custom virtual network, the cluster must use a user-assigned managed identity that has the *Network Contributor* role on the virtual network. If needed, assign the identity:++    ```azurecli+    az aks update \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --enable-managed-identity \+        --assign-identity "${IDENTITY_RESOURCE_ID}" \+        --yes+    ```++    Replace `IDENTITY_RESOURCE_ID` with the resource ID of your user-assigned managed identity. For more information, see [Use a user-assigned managed identity](../user-assigned-managed-identity).+3. **API server subnet**: Create a dedicated subnet for the API server in the same virtual network as your nodes. The subnet must be separate from your node subnet, be at least `/28`, and be delegated to `Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters`.++    For an AKS-managed virtual network, create the subnet in the virtual network in the node resource group:++    ```azurecli+    export VNET_NAME=$(az network vnet list --resource-group "${NODE_RESOURCE_GROUP}" --query "[0].name" --output tsv)++    export APISERVER_SUBNET_ID=$(az network vnet subnet create \+        --resource-group "${NODE_RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --vnet-name "${VNET_NAME}" \+        --name apiserver-subnet \+        --address-prefixes "<unused-address-range>" \+        --delegations Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters \+        --query id --output tsv)+    ```++    For a custom virtual network, create the subnet in your own virtual network instead, and set `APISERVER_SUBNET_ID` to its resource ID.+4. **API Server VNet Integration**: Enable API Server VNet Integration with the subnet you created, and then restart the cluster:++    ```azurecli+    az aks update \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --enable-apiserver-vnet-integration \+        --apiserver-subnet-id "${APISERVER_SUBNET_ID}"++    az aks stop --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}"+    az aks start --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}"+    ```++    For more information, see [Convert an existing AKS Standard cluster to API Server VNet Integration](../api-server-vnet-integration#convert-an-existing-aks-standard-cluster-to-api-server-vnet-integration).+5. **Network dataplane**: Update the network dataplane to Cilium. This command also sets the network policy to Cilium.++    ```azurecli+    az aks update \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --network-dataplane cilium+    ```++    For more information, see [Azure CNI Powered by Cilium](../azure-cni-powered-by-cilium).++Important++Update the network dataplane before you enable Auto node provisioning mode in the next section. After Auto mode is enabled, you can't change the network dataplane.++### Prepare the system node pool and node provisioning++1. **Ephemeral OS disk**: The system node pool must use an ephemeral OS disk. Check the current OS disk type:++    ```azurecli+    az aks nodepool list \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --cluster-name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --query "[?mode=='System'].{name:name, osDiskType:osDiskType}" \+        --output table+    ```++    You can't change the OS disk type of an existing node pool. If your system node pool uses a `Managed` OS disk, [add a new system node pool](../create-node-pools) with `--mode System --node-osdisk-type Ephemeral --os-sku AzureLinux --ssh-access disabled`, move your system workloads to it, and then [delete the old node pool](../delete-node-pool). You can then skip the next step.+2. **OS SKU and SSH access**: Update the system node pool to use Azure Linux and disable SSH access:++    ```azurecli+    az aks nodepool update \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --cluster-name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --name "<system-node-pool-name>" \+        --os-sku AzureLinux \+        --ssh-access disabled \+        --yes+    ```++    This command reimages the node pool. Wait for it to finish before you make other changes to the node pool. For more information, see [Use the Azure Linux Container Host](../use-azure-linux) and [Manage SSH access on AKS cluster nodes](../manage-ssh-node-access).+3. **Node provisioning mode**: Enable Auto node provisioning mode:++    ```azurecli+    az aks update \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --node-provisioning-mode Auto+    ```++    After you enable Auto mode, you can't revert to Manual mode without first removing all autoprovisioned nodes. For more information, see [Node auto-provisioning](../node-auto-provisioning).++### Enable required features and add-ons++1. Update the cluster tier to Standard, and enable the Azure Policy and Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider add-ons with secret rotation:++    ```azurecli+    az aks update --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" --tier standard++    az aks enable-addons \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --addons azure-policy,azure-keyvault-secrets-provider \+        --enable-secret-rotation+    ```+2. Enable the remaining required features:++    ```azurecli+    az aks update \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --auto-upgrade-channel stable \+        --node-os-upgrade-channel NodeImage \+        --enable-workload-identity \+        --enable-oidc-issuer \+        --enable-aad \+        --enable-azure-rbac \+        --disable-local-accounts \+        --enable-image-cleaner \+        --enable-vpa \+        --enable-keda \+        --yes+    ```++### Lock down the node resource group++Set the node resource group restriction level to `ReadOnly`. Do this step last, because lockdown blocks changes to resources in the node resource group, including the API server subnet you created earlier.++```azurecli+az aks update \+    --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+    --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+    --nrg-lockdown-restriction-level ReadOnly+```++For more information, see [Node resource group lockdown](../node-resource-group-lockdown).++### Migrate the cluster to AKS Automatic++If any requirement is still unmet, the migration command fails and lists the unmet requirements it detected. Some checks run only after earlier ones pass, so resolve the listed items and run the command again until it succeeds.++#### AKS-managed virtual network++```azurecli+az aks update \+    --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+    --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+    --sku automatic \+    --enable-hosted-system+```++#### Custom virtual network++Provide a subnet for the managed system node pool by using the `--system-node-subnet-id` parameter. For subnet requirements, see [Migrate an existing AKS Automatic cluster to managed system node pools](aks-automatic-managed-system-node-pools-about#migrate-an-existing-aks-automatic-cluster-to-managed-system-node-pools-preview). The `--node-subnet-id` parameter is optional. If you don't provide it, AKS uses the existing system node pool subnet.++```azurecli+az aks update \+    --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+    --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+    --sku automatic \+    --enable-hosted-system \+    --system-node-subnet-id "${SYSTEM_NODE_SUBNET_ID}" \+    --node-subnet-id "${NODE_SUBNET_ID}"+```++### Verify the migration++1. Confirm that the cluster uses the `automatic` SKU and `Standard` tier, and that the update finished successfully:++    ```azurecli+    az aks show \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --query "{sku:sku, provisioningState:provisioningState}" \+        --output json+    ```++    Confirm `sku.name` is `Automatic`, `sku.tier` is `Standard`, and `provisioningState` is `Succeeded`.+2. Confirm the cluster uses managed system node pools:++    ```azurecli+    az aks show \+        --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \+        --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}" \+        --query hostedSystemProfile \+        --output json+    ```++    Confirm `hostedSystemProfile.enabled` is `true`. For a custom virtual network, `systemNodeSubnetId` and `nodeSubnetId` show your subnet resource IDs. For an AKS-managed virtual network, these values are `null`.+3. Get credentials for the cluster and confirm all nodes are in the `Ready` state:++    ```azurecli+    az aks get-credentials --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" --name "${RESOURCE_NAME}"+    kubectl get nodes -o wide+    ```++### Failure behavior++If migration can't provision managed system pool infrastructure (for example, because of regional capacity constraints), AKS preserves existing system and user node pools in their pre-migration state.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      @@ -2,13 +2,6 @@  This article provides best practices for monitoring and interpreting GPU signals on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). Instead of looking at NVIDIA GPU metrics in isolation, you correlate signals across utilization, memory, and workload context to improve long-term performance and node efficiency. -Important--AKS preview features are available on a self-service, opt-in basis. Previews are provided "as is" and "as available," and they're excluded from the service-level agreements and limited warranty. AKS previews are partially covered by customer support on a best-effort basis. As such, these features aren't meant for production use. For more information, see the following support articles:--- [AKS support policies](/en-us/azure/aks/support-policies)-- [Azure support FAQ](/en-us/azure/aks/faq)- ## Understand GPU utilization versus saturation  Don't treat the NVIDIA DCGM metric `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL` as a direct efficiency score. `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL` only indicates how often kernels are active, so it doesn't tell you whether the workload is compute-efficient. You get more accurate guidance by correlating utilization signals instead of reading them independently. Compare `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL` with `DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE`, and then compare `DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE` with `DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE` to identify whether your bottleneck is compute, memory, or launch and synchronization overhead.
